LazyMem: Retrieve Broadly, Construct Selectively for Efficient Long-Term Agent Memory

Jing Yu Affiliation: School of Data Science and Engineering, East China Normal University    Yibo Zhao Affiliation: School of Data Science and Engineering, East China Normal University    Jiaming Zhang Affiliation: School of Data Science and Engineering, East China Normal University    Xiang Li ††thanks: Corresponding author: xiangli@dase.ecnu.edu.cn Affiliation: School of Data Science and Engineering, East China Normal University
Abstract

Long-term memory lets LLM agents reuse past interactions, but raw dialogue histories are verbose and information-sparse. Retrieving broadly improves evidence coverage yet overwhelms downstream reasoning with noise; compressing at write time reduces noise but irreversibly discards details the future query may need. We introduce LazyMem, which sidesteps this dilemma by deferring all memory construction to query time. A lightweight 4B model processes the retrieved candidate pool in overlapping parallel windows, selectively retaining and compressing only query-relevant content. The model is trained through supervised fine-tuning followed by group-based reinforcement learning with a format-gated composite reward that combines a rule-based action signal measuring selection accuracy with an LLM-judged quality signal measuring source faithfulness and query utility. On the LongMemEval benchmark, LazyMem-4B achieves an LLM-judge accuracy of 0.85 with only 213 memory tokens, 68.7×\times fewer than retrieval-only, and generalizes to LoCoMo (0.68) without target-domain training, while reducing mean latency over the prior query-time baseline. The 32B variant reaches 0.93, surpassing oracle-context references on aggregation-heavy question types. The code associated with this work is publicly available at https://github.com/allacnobug/LazyMem.

1 Introduction

By maintaining long-term memory, LLM agents can preserve past exchanges with users and leverage them in subsequent conversations (Park et al., 2023; Packer et al., 2024; Zhong et al., 2024). However, the accumulated dialogue history can far exceed the context window, and including it indiscriminately buries relevant evidence in noise. The agent must therefore retrieve a query-relevant subset of its history and incorporate it into the current context. This retrieval step mirrors RAG in purpose but differs in the quality and structure of the underlying corpus.

Conventional RAG assumes curated, information-dense passages (Lewis et al., 2020; Karpukhin et al., 2020), whereas raw agent memories are loosely structured and verbose, with salient facts scattered across interaction turns (Maharana et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2024). This mismatch creates a dilemma. Noise and fragmentation make query-relevant evidence difficult to retrieve, yet expanding the recalled pool to improve evidence coverage increases context burden and further dilutes salient information (Shi et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2024).

Most existing methods seek to mitigate this dilemma through a construct-then-retrieve paradigm. They summarize (Zhong et al., 2024; Fang et al., 2025), rewrite (Chhikara et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026), aggregate (Sun and Zeng, 2025; Li et al., 2026), or link raw interactions into structured memory units (Xu et al., 2026a; Xu et al., 2026b) before storage, and retrieve relevant units at query time. By compressing and organizing raw interactions in advance, this paradigm facilitates query matching and reduces the burden on downstream reasoning. However, because this memory construction process is necessarily query-agnostic, it may discard details that later prove relevant. An ablation study reported in AMA-Bench (Zhao et al., 2026) shows that, even when retrieval errors are excluded, models given constructed memories perform substantially worse than those given the corresponding gold interaction turns, exposing the information loss introduced during memory construction (see Appendix A for details).

A natural alternative is to preserve raw interactions and defer construction to query time. With the query available, the system can determine which facts to retain and how aggressively to compress them, avoiding the permanent information loss inherent in query-agnostic construction. Wu et al. (2026) provides a starting point with Query-Driven Pruning: raw conversations are retrieved, and a separate language model extracts query-relevant content through prompting before passing the resulting evidence to the answer model. This design demonstrates the feasibility of a retrieve-then-construct paradigm, where raw interactions are preserved, and evidence is constructed conditioned on the query. However, this approach has two limitations. First, although extraction is decoupled from answer generation, the trade-off between retrieval coverage and context burden remains. The extraction model still processes the entire recalled pool at once, leaving it vulnerable to context rot as salient evidence is diluted by lengthy, noisy context. Second, prompt-based extraction introduces an additional trade-off among extraction quality, cost, and latency. Large models can achieve reasonable extraction quality without task-specific training but are costly and slow, whereas lightweight models are cheaper and faster but perform poorly without dedicated training. Our experiments in Appendix B confirm these observations.

These findings motivate the central question of this work: how can agent memory systems balance information fidelity against context burden under practical cost and latency constraints?

We introduce LazyMem, a retrieve-then-construct agent memory system designed to address these trade-offs. Its name reflects two senses of laziness: it performs no lossy construction at write time, deferring memory construction until a query arrives, and it delegates construction to a lightweight memory-processing model, freeing the main reasoning model from processing raw memory. At query time, LazyMem first retrieves a large pool of raw observations to ensure adequate evidence coverage; the memory-processing model then constructs compact, query-conditioned evidence for downstream reasoning. To control context burden, it processes the recalled pool in overlapping windows, keeping each input short enough to mitigate context rot while preserving evidence across window boundaries. To achieve high construction quality despite its small size, we train it with reinforcement signals that jointly optimize fidelity to the original interactions and downstream reasoning utility. The windows are processed in parallel to bound latency as the recalled pool grows, while the model’s small size keeps inference cost low.

Our main contributions are as follows.

  • •

    We propose LazyMem, a retrieve-then-construct agent memory system that preserves raw interactions, retrieves broadly at query time, and constructs compact evidence through a lightweight model operating over overlapping parallel windows, avoiding irreversible write-time loss while bounding context length and latency.

  • •

    We train a 4B memory-processing model with SFT and format-gated reinforcement learning that jointly rewards selection accuracy, faithfulness, and query utility. Cumulative training raises the LLM-judge accuracy on the LongMemEval long-context memory benchmark from 0.41 (prompting alone) to 0.85.

  • •

    On two established benchmarks, LazyMem-4B delivers an LLM-judge accuracy of 0.85 on LongMemEval with 213 memory tokens (68.7×\times fewer than retrieval-only) and 0.68 on LoCoMo without any target-domain training, while reducing mean end-to-end latency over the prior query-time method.

2 Related Work

Early efforts such as MemoryBank (Zhong et al., 2024) and MemGPT (Packer et al., 2024) equip LLM agents with persistent memory beyond finite context windows. Despite their different designs, these systems share a general pipeline that stores past interactions, retrieves information relevant to the current query, and incorporates the retrieved content into the model context. From the perspective of when past interactions are transformed into task-usable memory, we broadly organize existing approaches into two paradigms: construct-then-retrieve and retrieve-then-construct.

Construct-then-retrieve methods transform interactions into compact or structured memory representations before future queries are known. One line manages persistent memory through explicit operations, from prompt-based execution of a predefined set of ADD/UPDATE/DELETE operations (Chhikara et al., 2025) to operation policies learned via reinforcement learning (Yan et al., 2026; Yue et al., 2026) and reusable, evolvable memory skills (Zhang et al., 2026). Another organizes interaction history hierarchically, consolidating concrete interactions into temporal, topical, and relational structures at varying granularities and abstraction levels (Fang et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026a). On the retrieval side, mechanisms are tailored to these representations, including semantic links among atomic notes (Xu et al., 2026b), entity–relation graphs (Chhikara et al., 2025), hierarchical top-down search (Sun and Zeng, 2025), and searched modular memory architectures (Zhang et al., 2025a). Despite their effectiveness, their write-time construction is necessarily query-agnostic, creating a potential mismatch with unforeseen future information needs.

Retrieve-then-construct methods instead retain fine-grained records close to the original interactions and defer modeling to the construction stage, forming task-specific context by filtering, compressing, and reorganizing recalled content once the query is known. Although related ideas such as reranking (Yu et al., 2024), context compression (Xu et al., 2023), and query-focused summarization (Edge et al., 2024) are well studied in conventional RAG, this paradigm remains underexplored in agent memory. NanoMemory (Wu et al., 2026) preserves raw conversations and combines turn isolation retrieval with query-driven pruning to distill recalled sessions into compact, information-dense context. However, because it processes the entire recalled pool at once, context rot remains a challenge during memory construction. Moreover, its prompt-based constructor faces a trade-off between construction quality and inference efficiency.

Our LazyMem builds on this paradigm by formulating query-conditioned memory construction as a learned policy implemented by a lightweight model. It processes large candidate pools through overlapping windows in parallel, limiting the context handled in each construction step while controlling query-time latency.

3 Method

3.1 The LazyMem Pipeline

We consider the problem of answering a query qq over a long interaction history, where the agent must draw on relevant information scattered across past user and assistant messages. LazyMem addresses this as a lazy, retrieve-then-construct memory system (Figure 1): messages are stored verbatim with no processing at write time, and all work is deferred to query time, where the system operates in three stages.

Retrieve broadly.

LazyMem first builds a high-recall pool of at most nn candidate messages, ℛq\mathcal{R}_{q}, using standard hybrid retrieval. Dense (bi-encoder) and sparse (BM25) retrievers run in parallel on qq, and their ranked lists are merged via Reciprocal Rank Fusion (Cormack et al., 2009); a cross-encoder reranker then scores the fused candidates and retains the top nn. All retrieval components are off-the-shelf. The contribution of LazyMem lies in how the resulting pool is subsequently processed.

Construct selectively.

A construction module then compresses ℛq\mathcal{R}_{q} into a compact, query-conditioned memory context mqm_{q}. It partitions the pool into overlapping evidence windows and applies a lightweight, RL-trained memory-processing model πθ\pi_{\theta} to all windows in parallel (Section 3.2). Windowing keeps every model input short while preserving cross-boundary evidence, and parallelism bounds latency as the pool grows. Section 3.3 describes how πθ\pi_{\theta} attains high construction quality despite its small size.

Answer.

Finally, an answer model takes the query qq together with the compact context mqm_{q} to produce the prediction.

3.2 Query-Conditioned Memory Construction

Construction proceeds in two steps: a history windowing step that restores local conversational context around each retrieved message, and a memory-processing model that compresses each window into query-relevant content.

History windowing.

Messages in ℛq\mathcal{R}_{q} arrive stripped of their surrounding conversation, so processing them in isolation can break dialogue coherence. Resolving a pronoun in a retrieved message, for instance, may require the preceding turns. LazyMem therefore reconstructs local context directly from the interaction history. Let d1,…,d|ℛq|d_{1},\ldots,d_{|\mathcal{R}_{q}|} denote the retrieved messages in chronological order, and let idx⁡(⋅)\mathrm{idx}(\cdot) return a message’s position in the history. Each did_{i} is expanded into a span containing itself and the ww messages on either side. These neighbors supply interpretive context and often recover relevant information that retrieval missed. Two adjacent retrieved messages are merged into a single contiguous window whenever their spans overlap:

idx⁡(di+1)−idx⁡(di)≤2​w.\mathrm{idx}(d_{i+1})-\mathrm{idx}(d_{i})\leq 2w. (1)

Applying this rule transitively yields MM maximal windows with no duplicated context. Windows exceeding a maximum length LL are split into overlapping sub-windows, bounding the input length of every model call. We denote the final set of windows by {W1,…,WP}\{W_{1},\ldots,W_{P}\} with P≥MP\geq M, and analyze the effect of ww in Appendix C.4.

Memory-processing model.

The model πθ\pi_{\theta} processes each pair (q,Wj)(q,W_{j}) independently at the granularity of individual messages. For every message x∈Wjx\in W_{j}, it predicts an action αx∈{Keep,Drop}\alpha_{x}\in\{\textsc{Keep},\textsc{Drop}\}: a kept message is rewritten into a compressed form x~\tilde{x} that retains only query-relevant content, while a dropped message produces no output. When overlapping sub-windows predict the same message, we deduplicate by idx⁡(⋅)\mathrm{idx}(\cdot), preferring Keep and breaking ties by window order. The surviving compressions are then concatenated chronologically to form mqm_{q}, which is passed to the answer model together with qq.

3.3 Training the Memory-Processing Model

We train πθ\pi_{\theta} with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) followed by group-based reinforcement learning (RL).

Supervised fine-tuning.

We build SFT examples from source interactions whose messages carry gold and non-gold labels. Gold messages contain evidence required to answer the query, while non-gold messages do not. Using the candidate retrieval and history windowing described above, we present the query and each evidence window to an instruction-following teacher model, which performs the memory-processing task: it labels every message Keep or Drop and generates query-relevant compressed text for each Keep message. We discard an instance if the teacher drops a gold message, produces unparsable output, violates the schema, or returns a number of decisions that does not match the window size. Each retained example maps a query and one evidence window to the per-message actions and the compressions of all Keep messages. Supervised fine-tuning on these examples teaches the model the output format and basic Keep/Drop behavior, and the resulting checkpoint serves as the reference policy πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}. Full implementation details are reported in Section 4.1.

Group-based policy optimization.

Starting from πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}, we refine πθ\pi_{\theta} with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO; Shao et al. 2024), modified as below. Each prompt pp pairs the query qq with one evidence window. The sampling policy πθold\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}} generates GG candidate outputs {ok}k=1G\{o^{k}\}_{k=1}^{G}, and each receives a scalar reward rk=R⁡(ok,p)r^{k}=R(o^{k};\,p) from the composite reward of Eq. 6. Each output’s advantage is computed relative to its group:

A^k=rk−mean​{rl}l=1Gstd​{rl}l=1G+δ,\hat{A}^{k}=\frac{r^{k}-\mathrm{mean}\{r^{l}\}_{l=1}^{G}}{\mathrm{std}\{r^{l}\}_{l=1}^{G}+\delta}, (2)

where δ\delta is a small constant for numerical stability. For each generated token otko_{t}^{k}, we compute the importance-sampling ratio between the current and the sampling policy:

ρtk=πθ​(otk∣p,o<tk)πθold​(otk∣p,o<tk).\rho_{t}^{k}=\frac{\pi_{\theta}(o_{t}^{k}\mid p,\;o_{<t}^{k})}{\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(o_{t}^{k}\mid p,\;o_{<t}^{k})}. (3)

This ratio is clipped asymmetrically with lower and upper bounds ϵl\epsilon_{l} and ϵh\epsilon_{h}, yielding the per-token surrogate:

ltk=min⁡(ρtk​A^k,clip⁡(ρtk, 1−ϵl, 1+ϵh)​A^k).l_{t}^{k}=\min\!\bigl(\rho_{t}^{k}\,\hat{A}^{k},\;\mathrm{clip}(\rho_{t}^{k},\,1{-}\epsilon_{l},\,1{+}\epsilon_{h})\,\hat{A}^{k}\bigr). (4)

The asymmetric clipping and the token-level normalization below follow Decoupled Clip and Dynamic Sampling Policy Optimization (DAPO; Yu et al. 2025). Unlike DAPO, we retain the KL penalty from GRPO to keep the policy close to πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}, giving the objective:

𝒥(θ)=𝔼p,{ok}k=1G∼πθold[∑k=1G∑t=1|ok|ltk∑k=1G|ok|−βDKL(πθ∥πref)],\mathcal{J}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\,p,\;\{o^{k}\}_{k=1}^{G}\sim\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}}\!\left[\frac{\sum_{k=1}^{G}\sum_{t=1}^{|o^{k}|}l_{t}^{k}}{\sum_{k=1}^{G}|o^{k}|}-\beta\,D_{\mathrm{KL}}\bigl(\pi_{\theta}\,\|\,\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}\bigr)\right], (5)

which we maximize with respect to θ\theta. The surrogate is normalized at the token level across the whole group, dividing by the total token count ∑k|ok|\sum_{k}|o^{k}| rather than averaging per output, so that longer outputs are not down-weighted. The KL term DKLD_{\mathrm{KL}} uses the low-variance k3k_{3} estimator (Shao et al., 2024), with β\beta controlling its strength.

Reward design.

The reward gates a combination of an action reward RactR_{\mathrm{act}} and a quality reward RqualR_{\mathrm{qual}}, both normalized to [0,1][0,1], on format validity:

R(o;p)=𝕀[o∈𝒱](λactRact+λqualRqual).R(o;\,p)=\mathbb{I}[o\in\mathcal{V}]\left(\lambda_{\mathrm{act}}R_{\mathrm{act}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{qual}}R_{\mathrm{qual}}\right). (6)

An output is valid (o∈𝒱o\in\mathcal{V}) if it is a single JSON object that matches the prescribed schema, contains exactly one decision per message in the window, and supplies the required compressed content for each Keep message. Any output that fails one of these conditions receives zero reward. The weights λact,λqual\lambda_{\mathrm{act}},\lambda_{\mathrm{qual}} and their schedule are specified in the reward curriculum below.

Action reward.

We reuse the source dataset’s own annotations: messages marked as supporting evidence for the query are gold, the rest non-gold. For a message xx with predicted action αx\alpha_{x}, the per-message action score is defined as:

sx={rg,x​ gold,αx=Keep,−pg,x​ gold,αx=Drop,rn,x​ non-gold,αx=Drop,−pn,x​ non-gold,αx=Keep,s_{x}=\begin{cases}\phantom{-}r_{\mathrm{g}},&x\text{ gold},\;\alpha_{x}=\textsc{Keep},\\ -p_{\mathrm{g}},&x\text{ gold},\;\alpha_{x}=\textsc{Drop},\\ \phantom{-}r_{\mathrm{n}},&x\text{ non-gold},\;\alpha_{x}=\textsc{Drop},\\ -p_{\mathrm{n}},&x\text{ non-gold},\;\alpha_{x}=\textsc{Keep},\end{cases} (7)

where rg,pg,rn,pn>0r_{\mathrm{g}},p_{\mathrm{g}},r_{\mathrm{n}},p_{\mathrm{n}}>0 are reward and penalty magnitudes. This asymmetric design rewards keeping gold messages and dropping non-gold ones, and penalizes the converse. We compute the mean of sxs_{x} separately within the gold and non-gold categories, then average the means of whichever categories are present to obtain SactS_{\mathrm{act}}. Because this averages at the category level, gold and non-gold receive equal weight whenever both are present, so the more populous category cannot dominate SactS_{\mathrm{act}}. We then rescale SactS_{\mathrm{act}} to Ract∈[0,1]R_{\mathrm{act}}\in[0,1] using its minimum and maximum attainable values for that sample (Appendix E).

Quality reward.

The quality reward scores the kept set 𝒦={x:αx=Keep}\mathcal{K}=\{x:\alpha_{x}=\textsc{Keep}\}. It judges only the quality of what is kept, while whether keeping was the correct action is left to RactR_{\mathrm{act}}. An LLM judge rates each x∈𝒦x\in\mathcal{K} on two dimensions, both in {0,1,2}\{0,1,2\} for no, partial, and full: a faithfulness score fxf_{x}, measuring whether the compressed content is supported by the source message, and a utility score uxu_{x}, measuring its usefulness for answering the query. The full rubric and judge prompt are in Appendix E. The per-message quality score is defined as:

Q(x)=𝕀[fx>0]fx+ux4∈[0,1].Q(x)=\mathbb{I}[f_{x}>0]\,\frac{f_{x}+u_{x}}{4}\;\in\;[0,1]. (8)

The indicator gates on faithfulness. Fully unfaithful content (fx=0f_{x}=0) is unsupported by or conflicts with the source message, so it scores zero no matter how useful it seems. Partially faithful content (fx=1f_{x}=1) is still grounded in the source and only imprecise, so it stays above the gate but earns less than fully faithful content. Past the gate, faithfulness and utility add up, so a shortfall on either lowers the score gradually rather than as a hard pass or fail. These graded scores give GRPO’s advantage normalization (Eq. 2) more signal than a binary gate would. Averaging Q⁡(x)Q(x) over the kept messages gives the window-level reward:

Rqual={0,𝒦=∅,1|𝒦|​∑x∈𝒦Q⁡(x),otherwise.R_{\mathrm{qual}}=\begin{cases}0,&\mathcal{K}=\emptyset,\\[4.0pt] \displaystyle\frac{1}{|\mathcal{K}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{K}}Q(x),&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (9)

Reward curriculum.

The weights satisfy λact,λqual≥0\lambda_{\mathrm{act}},\lambda_{\mathrm{qual}}\geq 0 and λact+λqual=1\lambda_{\mathrm{act}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{qual}}=1, which keeps R∈[0,1]R\in[0,1] and fixes the reward scale as the weights change. We schedule them in two phases. The first phase sets (λact,λqual)=(1,0)(\lambda_{\mathrm{act}},\lambda_{\mathrm{qual}})=(1,0), relying only on the format gate and the inexpensive rule-based action reward. Once the validation format-validity rate exceeds a threshold τ\tau, training switches once to a fixed pair of preset weights with both components positive, and these weights are held constant for the rest of training. Deferring the LLM-judged quality reward this way lowers the cost of early training. The preset weights, τ\tau, the scoring rubric, the judge model, and all reward hyperparameters are given in Appendix E.

4 Experiments

Our experiments center on the trade-off studied in this paper: preserving useful memory information while controlling context overhead under practical cost and latency constraints. We organize the evaluation around four research questions.

RQ1 (Effectiveness): does LazyMem outperform competitive memory baselines, both in-domain and out-of-domain (Section 4.2)?

RQ2 (Efficiency): are these gains achieved with lower context overhead, as measured by inference latency and input tokens (Section 4.3)?

RQ3 (Ablations): how much do the cumulative SFT and RL training stages contribute beyond the prompt-only base constructor (Section 4.4)?

RQ4 (Further Analysis): where does LazyMem fail, and how do errors distribute across pipeline stages (Section 4.5)?

4.1 Experimental Setup

Datasets.

We evaluate on two long-context memory benchmarks. LongMemEval (Wu et al., 2024) contains 500 questions, each grounded in a long multi-session user–assistant history. Because our method requires training data, we split the dataset into 360/40/100 train/validation/test examples via stratified sampling over question types (Appendix D.1). All baselines are re-evaluated on our test split with the same answer model, so reported numbers are directly comparable to one another, though not to previously published full-set results. LoCoMo (Maharana et al., 2024) is used strictly for testing and is excluded from both SFT and RL. Following Zhang et al. (2026), we evaluate category 1–4 questions from the last two conversations (314 questions). LongMemEval thus measures in-domain performance and LoCoMo measures out-of-domain generalization.

Training.

We use Qwen3-4B (Yang et al., 2025) as the base memory-processing model, and first apply supervised fine-tuning to teach it the memory-selection and compression format. The SFT data comes from 100 questions sampled from the LongMemEval training split (stratified by question type) and annotated by DeepSeek-V4-Flash (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2026). Because most messages in a window are non-gold evidence, correct annotations are dominated by Drop, so we balance the data at the window level to keep the model from favoring either action, yielding 776 SFT instances. Full construction and statistics are in Appendix D.2.

We then train with GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), using DAPO-style asymmetric clipping (Yu et al., 2025) and resampling the RL data to a 50/50 balance of prompts with and without gold evidence, so that the model gets enough gold-bearing windows to learn when to retain, not just when to drop (Appendix D.2). The reward combines the rule-based action reward RactR_{\mathrm{act}} and the LLM-judged quality reward RqualR_{\mathrm{qual}} under the format gate of Eq. 6, following the two-phase curriculum of Section 3.3. Hyperparameters for both stages are given in Appendix D.3.

Baselines.

We compare LazyMem against methods spanning the main memory-construction paradigms. (i) Oracle references: Oracle Turn and Oracle Session supply the gold evidence turn or session directly to the answer model, and serve as reference points. (ii) Retrieval without construction: RAG Top20/Top50 use the same hybrid retrieval as LazyMem (Section 3.1), then concatenate the top results in chronological order without further processing. (iii) Construct-then-retrieve: systems that build or update memory before the query arrives. This includes the training-free LightMem (Fang et al., 2025), StructMem (Xu et al., 2026a), Mem0 (Chhikara et al., 2025), and MemoryBank (Zhong et al., 2024), and the trained MemSkill (Zhang et al., 2026) and MemT (Yue et al., 2026). (iv) Retrieve-then-construct: NanoMemory (Wu et al., 2026), which stores raw messages and constructs query-relevant context at inference time, the same paradigm as LazyMem. Unless otherwise specified, baselines use Qwen3-32B with thinking mode enabled as the memory-processing model that constructs each system’s memory; for LazyMem we report both a Qwen3-32B (Yang et al., 2025) variant and our trained LazyMem-4B model. Configurations and prompts are provided in Appendix D.4.

Retrieve and answer model.

For LazyMem, we retrieve a candidate pool of k=50k{=}50 messages with the hybrid retrieval pipeline of Section 3.1, using Qwen3-Embedding-8B (Zhang et al., 2025b) for dense embeddings, Okapi BM2511 1 https://github.com/dorianbrown/rank_bm25 for sparse retrieval, and BGE-Reranker-v2-M322 2 https://huggingface.co/BAAI/bge-reranker-v2-m3 for reranking, and expand each message with a context window of radius w=2w{=}2. Except where noted, all methods share the same frozen answer model, Qwen3-32B with thinking mode enabled, so that performance differences reflect memory quality alone.

Metrics.

Our primary metric is an LLM-as-a-judge (LJ) score (Zheng et al., 2023). Specifically, DeepSeek-V4-Pro compares each prediction against the reference answer and assigns a binary correctness label. We report the average LJ score for each dataset, along with a breakdown by question type. For the efficiency analysis (RQ2), we measure two quantities: the online end-to-end per-query latency and the total number of input tokens processed by the answer model. Further measurement details are provided in Appendix C.2.

4.2 Main Results (RQ1)

Table 1 answers RQ1 affirmatively: LazyMem achieves the best overall performance both in-domain and out-of-domain. On LongMemEval, LazyMem with Qwen3-32B reaches an LJ of 0.93, 0.11 above the strongest non-oracle baseline (StructMem, 0.82), and LazyMem-4B still tops every baseline at 0.85. On LoCoMo, the 32B variant again leads (0.69) and the 4B variant follows at 0.68 without any LoCoMo training data, yet ahead of the LoCoMo-trained MemT and MemSkill. The strongest query-time methods outperform the strongest write-time ones on both benchmarks.

Where the gains come from, and why they can exceed oracle context.

The gains concentrate on aggregation- and temporal-oriented types. On KU and MS, the 32B variant reaches 1.00 and 0.93, improving over the best baseline by 0.12 in both. On MS and TR, it even exceeds both gold-context oracles, whose own scores stay well below saturation (Oracle Turn: 0.85/0.69; Oracle Session: 0.81/0.65). This is possible because a single oracle turn or session cannot contain evidence scattered across multiple sessions, and providing the full session in fact introduces noise. Query-time construction sidesteps both problems by filtering retrieved context conditioned on the question, removing noise while preserving cross-session evidence for downstream reasoning. On single-fact types (KU, SSA, SSU), where oracle context is already sufficient, both LazyMem and the oracles saturate near 1.00. The only type where LazyMem trails the oracles is SSP (0.50 vs. 0.67). These questions ask for recommendations grounded in user history, a setting that favors persistent user profiles over on-demand evidence assembly: write-time methods (StructMem 0.83, Mem0 0.83) substantially outperform all query-time ones.

This effect appears on LongMemEval but not LoCoMo because of a difference in retrieval recall. As Table 9 shows, LongMemEval recall is near-complete (All@50 = 0.99), so the bottleneck is noise and filtering alone suffices to outperform gold-context baselines. On LoCoMo, recall is lower (All@50 = 0.89): filtering helps but cannot recover missing evidence, limiting gains to matching rather than exceeding oracle performance. Write-time methods trail on both benchmarks because they do not filter the retrieval pool at query time, leaving noise in the QA context regardless of recall.

The lightweight 4B variant ranks top-two on five of six LongMemEval types; the sole exception is MS, and the overall 32B→\rightarrow4B drop (0.93→\rightarrow0.85) comes almost entirely from this type (0.93→\rightarrow0.67). We analyze the MS gap in conjunction with the error attribution in Section 4.5.

4.3 Efficiency Analysis (RQ2)

Figure 2 shows that LazyMem offers a strong accuracy–context trade-off, with both configurations lying on the token–accuracy Pareto frontier. LazyMem-4B achieves an LJ of 0.850.85 with an average of only 213 memory tokens, reducing the token count by factors of 68.768.7 relative to RAG Top50 and 21.021.0 relative to StructMem, while improving LJ by 0.100.10 and 0.030.03, respectively. Using the Qwen3-32B constructor further increases LJ to 0.930.93 with 1,041 tokens. These results suggest that constructing evidence conditioned on the query can reduce the context passed to the answer model without sacrificing relevant information (Table 6).

The latency results show that LazyMem-4B also provides a favorable accuracy–latency trade-off. Although it has higher online latency than the write-time methods LightMem and StructMem, it achieves higher accuracy. Compared with Nano Memory, the other query-time construction method, LazyMem-4B improves LJ from 0.800.80 to 0.850.85 while reducing mean end-to-end latency from 55.35 s to 40.86 s, placing it on the latency–accuracy Pareto frontier. Its lightweight trained constructor and parallel processing of recalled-history windows keep the additional query-time overhead manageable (Table 7).

4.4 Ablation Studies (RQ3)

Table 2 shows that cumulative training consistently improves the constructor over prompting alone. The final RL model raises LJ from 0.41 to 0.85 on LongMemEval and from 0.56 to 0.68 on LoCoMo. Most of the initial gain comes from SFT, which improves LJ by 0.31 and 0.07, respectively, while sharply increasing Gate Fmt. from 0.397 to 0.963 and from 0.622 to 0.985. This suggests that a substantial portion of the SFT gain is associated with eliminating malformed or misaligned gate outputs, although format compliance alone does not guarantee semantically correct decisions.

RL further improves LJ by 0.13 and 0.05, with the largest gains on LongMemEval SSP, TR, and MS. Since Gate Fmt. increases only marginally to 0.997 on both benchmarks, these gains cannot be explained solely by formatting improvements. This pattern supports the effectiveness of our staged training design: SFT first establishes reliable gate execution, while RL subsequently refines task-relevant memory construction and improves downstream performance beyond format compliance.

4.5 Further Analysis (RQ4)

We open the pipeline to locate where LazyMem fails. Each incorrect answer is classified by the first stage that breaks: (i) retrieval miss, where gold evidence never enters the candidate set; (ii) editing loss, where evidence is retrieved but dropped or distorted during memory construction; and (iii) QA reasoning error, where the constructed memory contains the necessary facts but the answer model errs.

Overall distribution.

The error counts below exclude judge noise identified through human evaluation (Appendix F.3). Table 3 summarizes the results. On LongMemEval, both variants share the same retriever and achieve near-complete recall (All@50 = 0.99), so retrieval misses are absent. Editing loss dominates: 87% (13/15) of LazyMem-4B errors and all 7 of the 32B errors stem from the constructor dropping or distorting answer-critical facts. Pure QA reasoning errors are rare (13% for 4B, 0% for 32B), indicating that once evidence survives into the final memory, the downstream model almost always answers correctly.

On LoCoMo, where conversations are longer and retrieval recall is lower (All@50 = 0.89), retrieval miss re-emerges as a substantial factor: 40% of 4B errors (24/60) and 42% of 32B errors (26/62). The remaining errors split between editing loss (20% for 4B, 13% for 32B) and QA reasoning (40% for 4B, 45% for 32B). Per-type breakdowns and representative cases are provided in Appendix F.

The 4B multi-session gap.

Section 4.2 noted that the 32B→\rightarrow4B drop on LongMemEval comes almost entirely from MS (0.93→\rightarrow0.67). Since both variants share the same retriever, this gap must originate in editing or reasoning. Per-type attribution confirms it: the 4B editor commits 8 editing-loss errors on MS versus only 1 for 32B (Appendix F.1). The 4B model more frequently drops evidence fragments that are individually tangential but collectively necessary for cross-session aggregation. The ablation reinforces this: MS is the only type where RL yields modest improvement (0.56→\rightarrow0.67) despite format saturation, while TR jumps from 0.65 to 0.88 and SSP from 0.17 to 0.67, suggesting the bottleneck is model capacity for cross-session evidence integration.

Detailed per-type breakdowns, representative case studies, and a manual audit of LLM judge noise are provided in Appendix F.

5 Conclusion

We presented LazyMem, a retrieve-then-construct agent memory system that defers all memory construction to query time. By processing recalled history in bounded, overlapping parallel windows with a lightweight RL-trained model, LazyMem simultaneously achieves high information fidelity and extreme context compression.

The core finding is that query-conditioned construction enables a 4B model to match or surpass much larger write-time systems. On LongMemEval, the 4B constructor reaches an LLM-judge accuracy of 0.85 with only 213 memory tokens, 68.7×\times fewer than standard retrieval, and the 32B variant reaches 0.93, surpassing oracle-context references on aggregation-heavy question types. On LoCoMo, LazyMem achieves 0.68/0.69 without target-domain training, outperforming baselines that do train on that benchmark.

Error attribution shows that the retrieval and answer-model stages are largely saturated, and that remaining gains concentrate in the construction stage. This positions memory-processing model scaling and richer training signals as promising directions for pushing query-conditioned memory systems further.

Appendix A AMA-Bench Needle Diagnostic

To better understand where information is lost in a memory-augmented system, we report the needle diagnostic introduced by Zhao et al. (2026). Table 4 reproduces the results reported in the original work; we do not rerun the corresponding experiments. The diagnostic evaluates the same needle-containing examples under three input conditions that differ only in the information exposed to the answering model: the original observations containing the needle, the memories constructed from those observations, and the memories returned by the complete retrieval pipeline. The decrease from Full Obs. w/ Needle to Constructed Mem. w/ Needle measures information loss introduced during memory construction, before retrieval is involved. This construction loss is substantial for all four methods, ranging from 19.6%19.6\% for HippoRAG2 to 41.3%41.3\% for MemoryBank, indicating that relevant evidence may be omitted, compressed, or altered when raw observations are converted into persistent memories.

Appendix B Effect of Retrieval Depth and Model Scale in Nano Memory

Table 5 studies the effects of retrieval depth and memory-construction model scale in Nano Memory, while fixing Qwen3-32B as the answer model. For the LongMemEval latency measurements, we use a server equipped with two NVIDIA A800 80GB PCIe GPUs and AMD EPYC 7763 CPUs. The memory-construction model is served with vLLM on one A800 GPU using bfloat16 precision, a GPU memory utilization of 0.9, batch size 1, and concurrency 1, while question embeddings are computed on the other GPU. We discard three warm-up runs and report statistics over three subsequent runs.

Increasing top-kk improves evidence coverage but also introduces more tokens for the construction model to filter. On LongMemEval, the 32B model improves from 0.710.71 at Top-3 to 0.800.80 at Top-10, whereas the 4B model peaks at Top-5 and then declines. A similar pattern appears on LoCoMo: the 32B model improves up to 0.730.73, while the 4B model peaks at Top-20 and degrades under deeper retrieval. This suggests that the larger construction model handles longer and noisier retrieved contexts more effectively.

The improved filtering quality comes at a higher computational cost. On LongMemEval, the 32B model requires 26.6426.64–40.7440.74 seconds of filtering latency on average, compared with 16.9516.95–19.5419.54 seconds for the 4B model. The performance gap is largest at Top-10, where the retrieved context is longest. Nano Memory therefore exhibits a clear trade-off among retrieval coverage, filtering quality, context size, and latency.

Appendix C Efficiency and Ablation: Details and Additional Results

C.1 Context overhead

Table 6 reports the exact number of memory tokens provided to the answer model. Compared with retrieval-based and most write-time construction methods, LazyMem substantially reduces the answer-input context while maintaining stronger accuracy. The LazyMem-4B variant is particularly compact, using only a few hundred memory tokens per question on both benchmarks. Nano Memory produces an even shorter context, but at a substantially lower accuracy, as shown in Figure 2.

C.2 Latency protocol and breakdown

All latency experiments run on a server with two NVIDIA A800 80GB PCIe GPUs and AMD EPYC 7763 CPUs. We serve LLM inference with vLLM on one GPU using bfloat16 precision and a GPU memory utilization of 0.9, and compute question embeddings on the other. Each method uses its own configured model size.

We evaluate questions one at a time, with no batching or parallelism across questions. For LazyMem, the independent history windows within a single question are processed concurrently (up to 64 at a time), exploiting the intra-query parallelism afforded by its construction procedure. We discard three warm-up runs and report statistics over the next three runs.

Table 7 breaks end-to-end latency down into retrieval, memory processing, and answer generation. Query-time methods add a memory-processing stage.

C.3 Retrieval and Reranking

Table 8 examines the effects of query formulation, dense–sparse retrieval, sparse-document representations, and CrossEncoder reranking. Unless otherwise specified, we use Qwen3-Embedding-8B (Zhang et al., 2025b) to produce dense embeddings and BGE-Reranker-v2-M333 3 https://huggingface.co/BAAI/bge-reranker-v2-m3 for reranking.

Combining dense and sparse retrieval generally improves gold-evidence coverage, while reranking further improves the quality of the top-ranked results. Query rewriting and LLM-generated tags provide additional gains in some configurations, but incur extra LLM inference costs.

We adopt configuration #15 in the main experiments. It uses the original query, combines dense retrieval with sparse retrieval over the raw memory text, and applies CrossEncoder reranking. This configuration achieves retrieval quality close to the best variants without requiring query rewriting or LLM-based tag generation. The prompts used for query understanding and tag generation were not extensively tuned; therefore, the corresponding results should be regarded as indicative rather than definitive comparisons of these techniques.

C.4 History-window radius

Table 9 evaluates the amount of neighboring history included around each retrieved item. Increasing the radius consistently improves evidence coverage, while the overall answer quality saturates after w=2w=2. This indicates that a limited amount of local conversational context is sufficient to recover most of the useful information, with larger windows providing only marginal additional gains.

Appendix D Experimental Setup Details

D.1 Dataset and Split Construction

LongMemEval (Wu et al., 2024) contains 500 questions, each grounded in a long, multi-session user–assistant interaction history. The dataset defines six question types: single-session user, single-session assistant, single-session preference, multi-session, temporal reasoning, and knowledge update. Abstention questions are indicated by the suffix _abs in their question IDs and retain their original question types.

Because our method requires training data, we stratify the 500 questions by type and split them into 360/40/100 training, validation, and test examples (72%/8%/20%). Within each type, examples are sorted by question ID and shuffled with a fixed seed of 42, while the largest-remainder method is used to preserve the original type distribution.

Table 10 reports the resulting per-type counts. The test split is excluded from SFT and RL training, hyperparameter tuning, and checkpoint selection. All model-selection decisions are based on the validation split, and the test split is used only for final evaluation.

D.2 Training Data

SFT data construction.

The 100 sampled questions yield 3,075 query–window pairs. We prompt DeepSeek-V4-Flash (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2026) in high-thinking mode with the prompt in Listing 1. For each message in a window, the teacher predicts a keep/drop decision and, when keeping, a compressed rewrite; its reasoning and structured decisions form the SFT target.

Since gold evidence is sparse within a window, the raw annotations are 3.92% keep and 96.08% drop. We discard 36 windows that drop gold evidence, then balance at the window level by pairing the 388 windows containing keep decisions with 388 sampled all-drop windows, giving 776 instances with average input and target lengths of 2,585 and 873 tokens. Automated validation finds no formatting errors in the raw annotations.

RL data balancing.

The raw RL training pool contains 11,072 query–window prompts, of which 8.98% contain gold evidence and 91.02% do not. We construct a balanced training set of 10,000 prompts by sampling 5,000 from each group: gold-containing prompts with replacement, non-gold prompts without.

D.3 Training Hyperparameters

Table 11 lists the full configuration of both training stages. SFT uses full-parameter fine-tuning with LLaMA-Factory (Zheng et al., 2024); RL uses GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) implemented in VERL (Sheng et al., 2025). Both stages train Qwen3-4B (Yang et al., 2025) on one node with two GPUs. SFT takes approximately 0.36 hours. The RL stage consists of 936 optimization steps and takes approximately 7.5–8.5 days in an uninterrupted run, including periodic validation and checkpointing.

For SFT, the effective global batch size is computed as per-device batch size 11 times gradient accumulation steps 88 times 22 GPUs. For RL, the batch size denotes the number of prompts per training batch; each prompt is sampled with 8 rollouts. The RL actor uses PPO mini-batch size 16 and per-GPU micro-batch size 4. Rollout generation uses nucleus sampling with top-p=0.95p=0.95.

D.4 Implementation and Inference Details

Except where noted, all methods use Qwen3-32B with thinking mode enabled as both the memory-processing model that constructs each system’s memory and the answer model, consistent with the main text. The constructed memory is concatenated with the query and passed to the answer model; the answer prompt is shown in Listing 3.

Baseline implementations.

We implement each baseline following its original or official pipeline, while standardizing the backbone model and retrieval budget where appropriate.

  • •

    Oracle Turn and Oracle Session. The answer model is given the gold evidence turn or the complete session containing it, respectively.

  • •

    RAG Top20 and RAG Top50. We retrieve the top-20 or top-50 messages per query using retrieval configuration #15 in Table 8, then concatenate them in chronological order before answer generation.

  • •

    LightMem (Fang et al., 2025). We use the original memory-entry construction and retrieval pipeline with hybrid user–assistant messages, retrieving the top-50 memory entries.

  • •

    StructMem (Xu et al., 2026a). We use the original pipeline with both structured summaries and memory entries, adopting hybrid user–assistant messages and retrieving the top-50 memory entries and top-5 structured summaries.

  • •

    Mem0 (Chhikara et al., 2025). We use the open-source Mem0 pipeline with Qwen3-Embedding-8B for dense retrieval and Qdrant as the vector store, retrieving the top-50 memories per query and otherwise following the official Mem0 benchmark configuration.

  • •

    MemoryBank (Zhong et al., 2024). We preserve the original MemoryBank design, including user-specific long-term memory banks, dated dialogue memories, event- and personality-level summaries, and FAISS indexing with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings at top-8 retrieval. This retains its native memory granularity rather than the unified retrieval granularity used for other baselines.

  • •

    MemSkill (Zhang et al., 2026). We use the controller checkpoint released by the original authors, trained on LoCoMo, and evaluate it zero-shot on our test split without retraining. Qwen3-32B serves as the executor, with the top-50 memories retrieved for answer generation.

  • •

    MemT (Yue et al., 2026). We follow the official inference setup using the released Mem-T-4B checkpoint, the default retrieval top-kk, and the original tool-calling and maximum tool-step settings. For LongMemEval we build the memory bank with the official pipeline; for LoCoMo we use the released prebuilt memory bank.

  • •

    NanoMemory (Wu et al., 2026). We use its query-time memory construction pipeline with session-level retrieval, and increase the retrieval depth from the original top-3 to top-10 for a stronger comparison.

D.5 LLM Judge

For both LongMemEval (Wu et al., 2024) and LoCoMo (Maharana et al., 2024), we adopt the official evaluation scripts and judge prompts released with the original papers, changing only the judge model. Concretely, the judge is DeepSeek-V4-Pro (OpenAI-compatible API at https://api.deepseek.com/v1, accessed in July 2026, temperature 0), which receives the question, reference answer, and model prediction, and outputs a binary correctness label. We do not modify the prompts, decision rules, or answer-matching logic of these scripts; we only substitute the underlying model.

Within each benchmark, the judge is applied uniformly to all systems and never observes which system produced a prediction. Note that although DeepSeek models are used both for SFT annotation and for judging, the judge is applied uniformly to all methods, so any bias affects all systems equally.

Appendix E Reward Details

This appendix supplements the reward design in Section 3.3 with the normalization of the action reward (Section E.1), the quality-reward rubric and judge configuration (Section E.2), and the complete reward hyperparameters (Section E.3).

E.1 Action Reward Normalization

The main text rescales the aggregate action score SactS_{\mathrm{act}} to Ract∈[0,1]R_{\mathrm{act}}\in[0,1] using its extreme attainable values; we give those bounds here. Both extremes occur when every message in a category receives the same action: SactS_{\mathrm{act}} is minimized by dropping all gold and keeping all non-gold messages, and maximized by the converse. Substituting the corresponding per-message scores (−pg,rg,−pn,rn-p_{\mathrm{g}},r_{\mathrm{g}},-p_{\mathrm{n}},r_{\mathrm{n}}; Eq. 7) into the category-level average yields SminS_{\min} and SmaxS_{\max}, and the normalized reward is

Ract=Sact−SminSmax−Smin∈[0,1].R_{\mathrm{act}}=\frac{S_{\mathrm{act}}-S_{\min}}{S_{\max}-S_{\min}}\;\in\;[0,1]. (10)

Since all magnitudes are positive, each category spans scmax−scmin=rc+pc>0s_{c}^{\max}-s_{c}^{\min}=r_{c}+p_{c}>0, so Smax>SminS_{\max}>S_{\min} for any non-empty window and the denominator never vanishes.

E.2 Quality Reward: Scoring Rubric and Judge Configuration

Judge model.

We compute the quality reward RqualR_{\mathrm{qual}} (Eq. 9) with Qwen-32B at temperature 0, capped at 1024 output tokens (180 s timeout, 3 retries, thinking enabled with a 512-token budget). The full judge prompt is given in Listing 2.

Faithfulness rubric.

The faithfulness score fxf_{x} grades whether the compressed content is grounded in the source message.

Utility rubric.

The utility score uxu_{x} grades how much the compressed content helps answer the query qq.

E.3 Reward Hyperparameters

Table 12 lists all reward hyperparameters. These values are set heuristically to encode relative preferences rather than calibrated costs: for instance, dropping gold evidence (pg=10.0p_{\mathrm{g}}=10.0) is penalized far more heavily than keeping a non-gold message (pn=1.0p_{\mathrm{n}}=1.0).

Appendix F Error Attribution Details

This appendix supplements Section 4.5 with per-type error breakdowns, representative case studies, and an assessment of evaluation reliability.

F.1 Per-Type Error Breakdown

The error counts below are computed after excluding judge noise identified in Section F.3. Tables 13 and 14 decompose errors by question type on LongMemEval and LoCoMo, respectively. Both variants share the same retriever on each benchmark.

On LongMemEval, the most striking contrast is on MS: the 4B editor produces 8 editing-loss errors versus 1 for 32B, confirming that the accuracy gap is localized to the editing stage. On LoCoMo, multi-hop errors are dominated by shared retrieval miss (33/46 across both variants); temporal errors concentrate in editing loss for the 4B model (7/18) and QA reasoning for the 32B model (13/19); single-hop errors are primarily QA reasoning failures (21/34).

F.2 Representative Case Studies

Table 15 presents representative cases for each failure type. Cases prefixed R denote retrieval miss, C denotes editing/compression loss, and Q denotes QA reasoning error.

F.3 Human Evaluation and Judge Noise Analysis

To assess the reliability of automatic evaluation, three expert annotators independently audit all LLM judge labels on both benchmarks, with final decisions determined by majority vote. For each benchmark, annotators inspect every judge-negative sample and cross-check judge-positive samples using entity, numerical, and cross-method consistency signals. On LoCoMo, we additionally identify 19 questions with gold-answer annotation errors that are excluded from all methods uniformly.

A false negative (FN) is a correct prediction judged incorrect; a false positive (FP) is an incorrect prediction judged correct. Table 16 reports the results for all 13 methods appearing in the main evaluation (12 on LoCoMo, as Oracle Session is not defined there).

LongMemEval.

Across 13 methods ×\times 100 questions = 1,300 labels, we identify 18 FN and 16 FP (overall noise rate 2.62%). False negatives and false positives are roughly balanced, so per-method corrections range from −2-2 to +5+5 percentage points. Both LazyMem variants have zero judge noise; their reported scores are exact. The relative ranking among all methods is unchanged after correction.

LoCoMo.

Across 12 methods ×\times 314 questions = 3,768 labels, judge noise is higher and strongly directional: of 294 flipped labels, 293 are false negatives and only 1 is a false positive (overall noise rate 7.80%). The raw judge therefore systematically underestimates all methods. The bias is consistent across methods (FN rates range from 4% to 12% per method), so relative rankings are preserved after correction. Additionally, we identify 19 questions where the gold answer itself contains annotation errors (wrong subject, incorrect date, or unsupported temporal claims); these are excluded from all methods uniformly and do not affect relative comparisons.

Sources of judge noise.

The dominant noise patterns, shared across both benchmarks, are:

  • •

    Semantically equivalent answers rejected due to surface-form differences (e.g., “3” vs. “3 weddings”, “45 minutes” vs. “45 minutes each way”).

  • •

    Keyword overlap masking factual errors, leading to false positives (e.g., correct entity mentioned alongside an incorrect temporal quantity).

  • •

    Relative temporal expressions (“last week”, “tomorrow”) not recognized as resolving to the gold date.

  • •

    Cautious qualifications (“no exact date is given”) causing the judge to ignore a preceding correct answer.

Impact on reported results.

All main results use raw LLM judge labels without manual correction to ensure reproducibility. The audit confirms that (1) judge noise does not change the relative ranking of any method on either benchmark, (2) the noise is conservative for LazyMem (zero FN on LongMemEval, FN-dominant on LoCoMo), and (3) the error attribution analysis in Section 4.5 excludes human-confirmed judge noise before classifying failures.
